summary: Defines the Session Description Protocol (SDP), a text format for describing multimedia sessions for announcement, invitation and other forms of session initiation. It tells endpoints what media to exchange and how to reach each other. It obsoletes RFC 4566 and is standards-track.

eli5.summary: Before a call begins, each side hands the other a short note saying what it can send and where. SDP is the format of that note, so every device can read it.

subtitle: The plain-text format that tells endpoints what media a session carries, where to send it and when it runs.

tldr.problem: Participants in a call, stream or conference need a standard way to learn the media types, transport addresses and timing of a session, whatever protocol delivers that information.
tldr.mechanism: SDP is a text format of single-letter lines (v=, o=, s=, c=, t=, m=, a= and others) in a fixed order, with a session-level section followed by zero or more media descriptions, extended through registered attributes.
tldr.outcome: SDP is only a description format, not a transport or a negotiation protocol. RFC 8866 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 4566.

today: RFC 8866 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2021. It obsoletes RFC 4566 and has not itself been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: What SDP Is For
sections.content:
When people start a teleconference, a voice-over-IP call or a streaming video, the participants need media details, transport addresses and other session metadata. The Session Description Protocol (SDP) is a standard representation for that information, regardless of how it is carried.

SDP is purely a format. It has no transport protocol of its own and is meant to ride on others, such as the Session Announcement Protocol, SIP, RTSP, email with MIME, and HTTP. It is also not meant to negotiate session content or media encodings; the RFC calls that outside the scope of session description.
sections.eli5: SDP is a form that says what kind of show is on, where to tune in and when. It does not deliver the form or argue about the details. It just writes them down.

sections.title: How SDP Gets Used
sections.content:
The RFC gives four example settings. With SIP, session descriptions travel in the messages that create sessions, and the offer/answer model gives a limited framework for negotiation using SDP. With RTSP, client and server use SDP syntax to describe media delivery parameters.

SDP can also be sent by email or on the web using the media type application/sdp, which lets a browser or mail reader launch the right application. Finally, a distributed session directory can periodically send descriptions of multicast sessions to a well-known multicast group; SAP is one protocol that does this, and SDP is the recommended format.
sections.eli5: The same note can be passed in a phone call setup, tucked in an email, put on a web page or posted on a notice board. The note looks the same each time.

sections.title: What a Description Must Convey
sections.content:
An SDP description includes the session name and purpose, the times the session is active, the media that make it up, and what is needed to receive those media (addresses, ports, formats). It may also carry bandwidth information and contact details for the person responsible.

For media it names the type (video, audio and so on), the transport protocol (for example RTP/UDP/IP) and the format. For IP multicast it gives the group address and port; for unicast it gives the remote address and port. Timing can be a list of start and stop times with repeats such as every Wednesday at 10am for one hour, and it is independent of local time zone.

Free-text subfields such as the session name use ISO 10646 in UTF-8 by default, though other character sets can be used. Internationalization applies only to those subfields, not to SDP as a whole.
sections.eli5: The note has to answer: what is it called, when is it on, what kinds of picture and sound are in it, and where do I tune in?

sections.title: Lines, Order and Sections
sections.content:
An SDP description is entirely textual: a series of lines of the form <type>=<value>, where the type is exactly one case-significant character. Lines end with CRLF, though parsers SHOULD also accept a single newline. The textual form was chosen for portability, and strict order and formatting rules mean most damage results in a malformed description that is easy to detect and discard.

A description has a session-level section that starts with v=, followed by zero or more media descriptions, each starting with an m= line. Session-level values are the default for all media unless a media-level value overrides them. Optional lines must still appear in the specified order.

The set of type letters is deliberately small and not extensible: a parser MUST ignore or reject a description with a type letter it does not understand. The a= attribute line is the main extension mechanism, and a parser MUST ignore any attribute it does not understand.

Any domain name in SDP MUST comply with RFC 1034 and RFC 1035, and internationalized domain names MUST use the ASCII Compatible Encoding form.
sections.eli5: Every line starts with one letter and an equals sign, and the lines must come in the right order, like a form with boxes in fixed places. If you meet a box you do not know, you skip it politely.

sections.title: The Core Lines
sections.content:
v=0 gives the version; this memo defines version 0 and there is no minor version. o= names the originator and carries a session ID and a session version, which must be increased whenever the description changes. The s= line is the session name and MUST NOT be empty; s=- is recommended when there is no meaningful name. Optional i=, u=, e= and p= lines give information, a URI, an email address and a phone number.

The c= line gives the network type, address type and connection address (IN, then IP4 or IP6). For IPv4 multicast a TTL MUST be present, in the range 0-255; for IPv6 multicast it MUST NOT be. The b= line proposes bandwidth, in kilobits per second by default, with the defined types CT (conference total) and AS (application specific).

The t= line gives start and stop times as decimal seconds since January 1, 1900 UTC. A stop time of zero means unbounded, and both zero means permanent. The r= line adds repeat times, and z= adjusts for time zone changes. The k= encryption key line is obsolete: it MUST NOT be included and MUST be discarded if received.
sections.eli5: The core lines say which version of the form this is, who wrote it, what it is called, how to reach it, how much room it needs and when it happens. One old line about secret keys is crossed out and must never be used.

sections.title: Media Descriptions and Attributes
sections.content:
Each m= line has the form m=<media> <port> <proto> <fmt> .... The media types defined are audio, video, text, application and message. The protocol can be udp, RTP/AVP, RTP/SAVP or RTP/SAVPF. For RTP, the format list holds payload type numbers in order of preference, and the first acceptable one SHOULD be used.

Attributes in a= lines come as a property (a=recvonly) or a value (a=orient:landscape), and every attribute MUST be registered with IANA. Section 6 defines a set, among them rtpmap (maps an RTP payload type, 0 to 127, to an encoding name and clock rate), fmtp (format-specific parameters), ptime and maxptime (packet time in milliseconds), framerate, lang and sdplang.

The direction attributes sendrecv, sendonly, recvonly and inactive set how media flows; if none is present, sendrecv SHOULD be assumed. The attributes cat and keywds are obsolete and SHOULD NOT be used.
sections.eli5: Each media line is one channel of the show, such as sound or picture, with a door number and a language it speaks. Extra notes called attributes add details like whether you only listen or also talk.

sections.title: Trust and Security
sections.content:
A session description cannot be trusted unless it was obtained over an authenticated and integrity-protected transport from a known and trusted source. Otherwise the media may not be the intended ones, the destination may be wrong, any parameter may be incorrect, or media security may be compromised. The endpoint may decide to ask the user whether to accept the session.

Software that parses a description MUST NOT be able to start any software other than what is configured to take part in multimedia sessions. A description arriving by announcement, email, invitation or web page MUST NOT put the user into an interactive session unless the user pre-authorized that. SDP MUST NOT be used to convey keying material (for example with a=crypto:) unless the delivery channel is both private and authenticated.

Intermediaries that modify descriptions, for instance to match NAT bindings, are NOT RECOMMENDED unless the authenticity and authority of the description can be checked. SDP alone cannot support those checks.
sections.eli5: A note you got from a stranger might be a trick. Do not let it start things on your computer or send your voice anywhere without your say-so.

sections.title: Changes From RFC 4566
sections.content:
RFC 8866 clarifies terminology and aligns it with the ABNF grammar in Section 9. It marks a=cat:, a=keywds: and k= as obsolete, expands the a=lang: and a=sdplang: specifications, and makes sending RTCP for inactive media streams mandatory.

It also removes the Private Sessions section, noting that the vast majority of uses of SDP is now establishing private sessions and that SAP has fallen out of widespread use. On the IANA side it changes how <fmt> values for UDP are registered and merges several attribute registries into a single <attribute-name> registry. The time-description syntax was revised to remove ambiguity, making a z= without a preceding r= a syntax error.
sections.eli5: This is the updated edition of the same form. Some old boxes were retired, some rules were made clearer, and the registry book was tidied.

v=0
o=jdoe 3724394400 3724394405 IN IP4 198.51.100.1
s=Call to John Smith
i=SDP Offer #1
u=http://www.jdoe.example.com/home.html
e=Jane Doe <jane@jdoe.example.com>
p=+1 617 555-6011
c=IN IP4 198.51.100.1
t=0 0
m=audio 49170 RTP/AVP 0
m=audio 49180 RTP/AVP 0
m=video 51372 RTP/AVP 99
c=IN IP6 2001:db8::2
a=rtpmap:99 h263-1998/90000

items.label: Origin
items.desc: Originator, session ID and session version.

items.label: Session name
items.desc: Exactly one per description; must not be empty.

items.label: Connection
items.desc: Network type, address type and connection address.

items.label: Bandwidth
items.desc: Proposed bandwidth, such as CT or AS, in kilobits per second.

items.label: Time active
items.desc: Start and stop times in seconds since 1900 UTC.

items.label: Repeat times
items.desc: Repeat interval, active duration and offsets.

items.label: Time zone adjustment
items.desc: Modifies the repeat lines it follows.
